For anyone who is looking to get this card, I recommend the 16GB version that comes with dual BIOS. If you google rx9060xt dual bios it'll provide a list of them. This small feature will unlock the card's full potential (sometimes with extra headroom).

This thing stock can handle most things at highest settings on 1440p without use of FSR/FG. If you enable OC mode on the physical card then you're looking at around 100-110fps on the more demanding titles and well over 120 on others. If yours don't come with a switch then you'll need to tweak it manually in Andrenalin to get the most out of it.

*Important Note* Only flip the bios switch when your pc is fully turned off. This is the only intended safe method of doing so. If you do it while it is on then it can lead to irreversible damages. Otherwise, cheers and enjoy!

@gateopssss  Well it's a free function for those with a dual bios card so it won't matter if people want to believe it or not. I just wanted to point it out for those who have this option so they can get the most out of it. We also most likely won't have the same exact specs since some have different cpus and motherboards, but this was the results I got. None of the above mentioned FSR or Fluid motion stuff was touched in the process. Just a simple flick of a switch and it now runs every game I own like a dream.

Just so we're all aware of the stock clock speed on this thing, it's around 2500-2700 (on paper) and then there's a max boost clock of 3300. Stock settings on quiet mode, you're more likely to see around 2500-2600 (some times it won't even touch these numbers) but I peak around 3200 after toggling OC along with -40UV & +10% draw. I know what FSR and FG is, I also know about the Andrenalin functions. None of those settings were touched besides just toggling the bios switch on the physical card itself. 

Also to clarify a bit more on my quiet mode settings' performance, I used the following tweaks: +250 Frequency offset, -40 undervolt, 2718 memory timing, +10% power limit. Even with these settings I was only getting ~60fps in ultra settings 1440p Cyberpunk. Returned the settings to default then powered off pc > toggled OC > boot up and straight into game > ~100fps. The only tunings I did after were same the undervolt and power limit draw. It really was just that simple.

Yeston 16gb Gaming Ace OC paired with a 7700x if people are still wondering. Not a top tier setup but the gains were impressive to me as well as I was running it stock for the first week before toggling it. I don't gain anything from mentioning this method along with the proper procedure on how to toggle it on and off (only when pc is turned off). Just mentioning a mostly overlooked feature for those that have it and want to get more gains out of their card.

comments.text: @Kalex-xe5wc  Not bad, but not great either.  The 8GB VRAM is fine for 1080p gaming, but may struggle with 1440p, especially when using frame gen.  At 1080p gaming, the CPU plays a big part, so having an 8/16 X3D CPU will help a lot, but the 5800X3D isn't exactly a powerhouse CPU by today's standards with lower boost clocks compared to Zen 5, and also being on DDR4, so I wouldn't be trying to max out the graphic settings, even @ 1080p.  But at the end of the day, you have your own PC and if it plays everything you want to play, that's all that matters.  The 5800X3D is still an excellent CPU for 1440p and 4K so you still have the option to upgrade your GPU in a couple of years when the next generation of GPU's are released and those entry to mid range GPU's are hopefully far more capable of 1440p/4K gaming compared to the current 8GB VRAM GPU's.  So basically...  Your PC is fine for 1080p (and some 1440p) gaming in 2025, but it may struggle in the coming years.  However, a new GPU in 2027 will probably be all you need to keep it going for another 3 years...  This is based on current AAA games.  If all you play are e-sports titles, you will be fine for another 5 years without upgrading.
